details:
**"Lines Composed a Few Miles Above Tintern Abbey"**
Wordsworth's meditative poem from 1798 about returning to the ruined abbey on the River Wye in Wales. It opens "Five years have past; five summers, with the length / Of five long winters!" The speaker "repose[s] / Here, under this dark sycamore," looks at "steep and lofty cliffs" and "hedge-rows," and imagines "some Hermit's cave." It ends by addressing his "dear, dear Sister," Dorothy.

**"I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud"**
Wordsworth's most famous lyric, often called "Daffodils." The speaker, wandering like a cloud that "floats on high o'er vales and hills," comes upon "a host, of golden daffodils," "Continuous as the stars that shine / And twinkle on the milky way," "tossing their heads in sprightly dance." He says "A poet could not but be gay, / In such a jocund company," and later the flowers "flash upon that inward eye / Which is the bliss of solitude," so that his heart "dances with the daffodils."

**Lyrical Ballads**
The 1798 collection Wordsworth published with Samuel Taylor Coleridge, often seen as the start of English Romanticism. Tintern Abbey closes the first edition; the 1800 edition added Wordsworth's famous Preface on poetry written in "the real language of men."

**Lucy poems**
A group of short lyrics about a mysterious girl named Lucy who has died, possibly inspired by Dorothy. They include "She dwelt among the untrodden ways," "Strange fits of passion have I known," "I travelled among unknown men," and "A slumber did my spirit seal," in which she "seemed a thing that could not feel / The touch of earthly years" and is now "Rolled round in earth's diurnal course."

**"The World Is Too Much With Us"**
A sonnet attacking materialism: "Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers; / Little we see in Nature that is ours; / We have given our hearts away, a sordid boon!" Because we are "out of tune" with nature, the speaker would "rather be / A Pagan suckled in a creed outworn," so he could feel less forlorn and see Proteus or "hear old Triton blow his wreathèd horn."

**"Ode: Intimations of Immortality from Recollections of Early Childhood"**
An 11-stanza ode about losing the visionary perception of childhood. Famous lines include "Whither is fled the visionary gleam? / Where is it now, the glory and the dream?", "Our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting," and "nothing can bring back the hour / Of splendour in the grass, of glory in the flower."

**Dorothy Wordsworth**
William's sister and close companion, whose Grasmere Journal describes the daffodils "tossing and reeling and dancing" that inspired "I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud." She is the "dear, dear Sister" of Tintern Abbey, and in "The Sparrow's Nest" William says of her, "She gave me eyes, she gave me ears; / And humble cares, and delicate fears."

**"London, 1802"**
A sonnet opening "Milton! thou shouldst be living at this hour: / England hath need of thee," lamenting the moral decline of England. G. K. Chesterton parodied it in a sonnet to Stilton cheese.

**"Composed upon Westminster Bridge"**
A sonnet about London at dawn that begins "Earth has not anything to show more fair." It ends with the city at rest: "Ne'er saw I, never felt, a calm so deep!" and "all that mighty heart is lying still!"

**The Prelude**
Wordsworth's long autobiographical poem in blank verse, subtitled "Growth of a Poet's Mind." Begun in 1798–99 and published after his death in 1850, it was meant as an introduction to a never-finished philosophical epic called The Recluse.

**The Excursion**
A long poem published in 1814 as the only completed part of The Recluse. It features characters called the Wanderer, the Solitary, and the Pastor. William Blake reportedly claimed that reading a passage from it gave him a bowel complaint that nearly killed him.

**"The Solitary Reaper"**
A poem about a "solitary Highland Lass" singing as she reaps grain. The speaker says "No Nightingale did ever chaunt / More welcome notes," and ends "The music in my heart I bore, / Long after it was heard no more."

**"Michael"**
A pastoral narrative poem from Lyrical Ballads about an old shepherd who risks losing his land and sends his son Luke to the city to earn money. Before Luke leaves, they lay the cornerstone of a sheepfold together; Luke falls into bad ways and never returns, and the sheepfold is left unfinished.

**"Resolution and Independence"**
A poem in which a despondent speaker meets an old leech-gatherer whose endurance restores him. It contains the lines "We Poets in our youth begin in gladness; / But thereof come in the end despondency and madness."

**"Ode to Duty"**
A poem addressing duty as "Stern Daughter of the Voice of God," containing the line "My hopes no more must change their name." Other clue poems include the sonnet "It is a beauteous evening, calm and free" and "Extempore Effusion upon the Death of James Hogg" ("How fast has brother followed brother, / From sunshine to the sunless land!").
